doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

title: Score pads versus Finale and the Heidelberg summers
summary: He sketches at the piano and uses Finale, which he mastered editing for Advance Music in Germany, then lost his chops during administrative work.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You obviously were in the era of using score pads and I’m wondering if you transitioned to Finale or Sibelius? You know actually I was in a colleague of yours, Dave Rivello’s music room and I was pleasantly surprised to see this big table with a huge pad on it and pencils. And he insisted it was important to do the physical act of putting a note on a piece of paper.

Uh huh, yeah. Well I do it both ways. I sketch stuff and figure out things on the piano, and then I use Finale also and you know, put it in. And I got pretty good on Finale and pretty fast, like because every summer I’d go to Germany and I was in charge of the Eastman Philharmonia, they had a gig there playing in Heidelberg at a castle there. And I didn’t have a piano so I had just the computer. And I edited a whole bunch of books and stuff, and I did a lot of editing for my publisher, Advance Music. And so I got pretty fast. But then I got more of an administrative job at Eastman around the year 2000 and it sort of worked into that a thing that I developed the Institute for Music Leadership and so I didn’t write any music for a long time. And man I lost my chops. I had to come back to it. And by then Finale had moved on and I was still back here in like a stage coach you know, and they’re driving cars you know. So you’ve got to keep your chops up there too.
